item.description:
Police have arrested Sumon, the main accused in the murder of 15-year-old Jannatul Tajmin, whose body was recovered from farmland in Lalmai upazila of Comilla, from Chittagong.
Comilla Superintendent of Police Md Anisuzzaman confirmed the arrest, saying police were investigating whether anyone else was involved. However, police have yet to recover the murdered student's mobile phone.
Tajmin's body was recovered from farmland beside Manumura Jungle in Jagatpur Uttarpara, Perul North Union, Lalmai upazila, around 8am on Thursday. A gamcha was wrapped around her neck.
Tajmin was the daughter of Abdul Alim, from the Chatiantala area of Churamonkati Union in Jeshore Sadar upazila. She lived with her family in a rented house in the Racecourse area of Comilla city.
After the post-mortem examination on Wednesday, her relatives took the body home. Earlier that night, her father, Abdul Alim, filed a murder case with Lalmai police station.
Tajmin left home on October 4, saying she was going to visit a friend. She had been missing since then, and her body was found in farmland four days later.

item.title: Mahalaya to mark countdown to Durga Puja across Bangladesh
item.description:
The countdown to Durga Puja, the largest religious festival of Bangladesh’s Hindu community, will begin with the celebration of Mahalaya across the country on Saturday.
Various religious and cultural programs will be organized at temples, including those in Dhaka, to mark Mahalaya, which heralds the advent of Goddess Durga.
Dhakeshwari National Temple will host a series of religious and cultural programs at dawn on Saturday.
Mahanagar Sarbajanin Puja Committee General Secretary Suvasish Kumar Biswas Sadhan said the Indian high commissioner in Dhaka is expected to attend the ceremony.
Ramna Kali Mandir will also host a large-scale Mahalaya celebration at dawn on Saturday, said Mintu Basu, a joint secretary of the temple management committee.
Mahalaya marks the end of Pitru Paksha, the dark fortnight dedicated to ancestors, and the beginning of Devi Paksha, the divine fortnight. Hindus pay homage to their deceased ancestors by performing puja and offering robes to Brahmins.
According to Hindu beliefs, Goddess Durga begins her journey from her home in Kailash to her paternal abode on Earth on this occasion, marking the approach of Durga Puja.
Dhaka University Jagannath Hall Upashanalaya Chief Priest Sadhan Chakrabarty said Goddess Durga would arrive on a horse (Ghotak) and depart by boat (Nauka) this year.
Bijaya Dashami falls on Wednesday, October 21, 2026. The goddess's departure by boat traditionally signifies abundant crops and rainfall, described as shasyashyamala vasundhara.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said Durga Puja would be held at 33,851 mandaps across the country this year, an increase of nearly 1,500 from last year.
Government funding for Durga Puja mandaps has also been increased to Tk 5 crore from Tk 4 crore following directives from Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, he said.
Meanwhile, the government has extended the Durga Puja holiday to 3 days through an executive order in response to longstanding demands from the Hindu community.
Combined with the regular Friday and Saturday weekend holidays, the extension will provide a total 5-day break from October 20 to 24.
Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad President Basudeb Dhar welcomed the decision.
"It's truly a positive decision. We thank the prime minister for such decision," he said.
Echoing Dhar, Mahanagar Sarbajanin Puja Committee General Secretary Suvasish Kumar Biswas Sadhan also expressed gratitude to the government, saying the 3-day holiday would allow Hindus to celebrate the festival with greater enthusiasm.
Sadhan said people traveling to their home districts would face no hassle this year because of the extended holiday.
However, he called for the government to make the 3-day Durga Puja holiday permanent from next year instead of announcing it through executive orders, saying this would recognize and fulfill the community's longstanding demand.
The Bangladesh Hindu Buddhist Christian Unity Council (BHBCUC) also welcomed the decision to declare 3 consecutive days of Durga Puja holidays.
"Through this, a long-standing demand of the minority communities has been fulfilled," said Manindra Kumar Natha, joint secretary general of the BHBCUC.
Preparations for the major festival of the Bengali Hindu community are underway across Bangladesh and elsewhere in the world. Durga Puja will formally begin with Maha Shashthi on October 16.
Puja committees, temples and mandaps across the country are completing preparations for the 5-day festival, including constructing and decorating pandals, installing idols, arranging lighting and preparing religious and cultural programs.
Authorities and local communities are also working to ensure security and smooth movement for devotees and visitors throughout the celebrations.
The festival will continue through Maha Saptami, Maha Ashtami and Maha Navami before concluding with Bijaya Dashami on October 21.
On the final day, devotees will bid farewell to Goddess Durga and take the idols in processions to designated rivers, ponds and other water bodies for immersion, known as Bisarjan.
Durga Puja holds deep religious and cultural significance for Bangladesh's Hindu community. It commemorates Goddess Durga's victory over the demon king Mahishasura and symbolizes the triumph of good over evil.
According to Hindu mythology, Mahishasura, empowered by a boon that made him invulnerable to men, became a threat to the gods. The gods combined their divine powers to create Goddess Durga, who fought and ultimately defeated him.
The main rituals will begin on Maha Shashthi with Kalparambha and Bodhan, the ceremonial awakening and unveiling of the goddess's idol.
Maha Saptami will feature the Nabapatrika, or Kola Bou, ritual, in which 9 plants representing different forms of the goddess are ceremonially bathed and worshipped.
Maha Ashtami will be marked by Sandhi Puja, performed at the transition between Ashtami and Navami, while Maha Navami will feature the concluding major worship rituals and bhog offerings.
As the festival approaches, mandaps in Dhaka and other parts of the country are taking shape with decorations, colorful lighting and artistic themes.
Devotees and visitors are expected to gather at the mandaps throughout the celebrations to offer prayers, receive prasad and participate in religious and cultural programs.
Observed as both a major religious occasion and an important part of Bangladesh's cultural heritage, Durga Puja brings together members of the Hindu community and people of other faiths, reflecting the country's tradition of communal harmony and peaceful coexistence.
Authorities will use a mobile application previously deployed by the National Telecommunication Monitoring Center (NTMC) to strengthen monitoring during Durga Puja.
The application will facilitate the rapid dissemination of information about any untoward incidents and help authorities respond quickly to maintain a peaceful environment during the celebrations, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said.
The Home Ministry has instructed the relevant authorities to ensure uninterrupted electricity supplies at puja venues.
Mandap organizers have been asked to keep generators on standby around the clock and maintain rechargeable lights as additional backup in case of power or generator failures.

item.title: People to bid final farewell to Toufique Imrose Khalidi Saturday
item.description:
People from all walks of life will pay their last respects to Toufique Imrose Khalidi, editor-in-chief of bdnews24.com and a pioneer of digital journalism in Bangladesh who died in London, on Saturday afternoon.
His body will arrive in Bangladesh from the United Kingdom on Saturday morning.
The coffin will then be taken to his residence, where family members and relatives will pay their last respects.
The body will be kept at the Banani Old DOHS playground from 2:00pm to 3:00pm, where friends, relatives, colleagues, well-wishers and representatives from different sectors of society will pay their final tributes.
His namaz-e-janaza will be held at the same venue at 3:00pm and later Toufique Imrose Khalidi will be laid to rest at the Martyred Intellectuals Graveyard in Mirpur at 5:00pm.
Meanwhile, his son Rad Sharar Khalidi has urged people across the country to pray for his father's eternal peace.
Toufique Imrose Khalidi passed away at a hospital in London on October 2 at the age of 59 following brain haemorrhage.
Born on June 14, 1967, Khalidi earned his master's degree in English Literature from Dhaka University before embarking on a career in journalism in 1989 with The Sunday Express.
Over a career spanning more than three decades, he held key positions across national and international media. He worked at the BBC World Service in London from February 2000 to June 2005.
Prior to that, he served at The Daily Star as Joint News Editor and Weekend Edition News Editor (1998-2000), Business Editor (1997-1998), and Diplomatic Correspondent (1991-1993), as well as Assistant Editor and Senior Correspondent at The Financial Express.
In the first half of 2005, Toufique Imrose Khalidi associated with bdnews24.com, pioneering Bangladesh's first internet-based 24/7 news service.
He received fellowships from the Journalists in Europe Foundation in Paris and the Japan Foreign Press Centre.
In 2014, he was named one of the “14 leading digital media innovators” across Asia-Pacific, Latin America, and West Asia at the South-to-South Media Dialogue in South Africa.
Toufique Imrose Khalidi chaired a UNESCO World Press Freedom Day event in 2016, attended the 2009 UN Climate Conference in Copenhagen as an observer, participated in the Global Media Forum in Bonn (2010, 2016, 2017, 2019), and spoke as a panelist at Harvard University’s "Bangladesh Rising" conference in 2018.
He also played a vital role in national policy formulation, serving on national committees for online media policy (2012, 2015), the news agency policy committee (2008), and the national task force for Dhaka river protection (2007).
In December 2017, the Bangladesh government conferred a special award on him on National ICT Day.

item.title: Case filed over attack on Nasiruddin Patwary in Kushtia
item.description:
A case has been filed against 20-25 unidentified people over the attack on Nasiruddin Patwary, chief coordinator of the National Citizen Party (NCP), at the Lalon Akhra in Kushtia.
Jannatul Ferdous Tony, convener of the NCP’s Kushtia district unit, filed the case with Kumarkhali Police Station on Wednesday; its Officer-in-Charge (OC), Jamal Uddin, confirmed on Friday afternoon.
According to the case statement, Nasiruddin Patwary visited the Chheuriya Akhrabari in Kumarakhali upazila on October 4 and listened to Lalon songs.
Around 8:15pm, as he and his associates were leaving through the main gate, a group of unidentified people attacked them. The statement alleged that one of the attackers threw an egg and a stone at the NCP leader before shouting.
It further alleged that the attackers, armed with sticks, bamboo poles, pipes, wooden battens, iron rods, stones and other locally available weapons, ambushed Nasiruddin Patwary and the NCP members accompanying him, leaving several people injured.
They took shelter inside the shrine to escape the attack, but the attackers followed them and continued to assault the group.
The attackers also allegedly vandalized Nasiruddin Patwary’s vehicle while attempting to prevent him from leaving the premises safely.
When local residents, NCP members and others intervened to protect the group, the attackers withdrew from the shrine and gathered near the main gate, where they continued to threaten and intimidate them, the complaint stated.
Later, with police assistance and in the presence of journalists, the NCP leader and other activists left the Akhrabari safely.
OC Jamal said no one has been arrested in connection with the incident so far.
Police were working to identify and apprehend those involved, he added.

item.title: Saudi says no Houthi truce until Yemen govt regains territory
item.description:
Saudi Arabia will not agree to a ceasefire with the Houthis until the Yemeni government that it backs regains all the territory it has lost in recent weeks, a regional source briefed on Saudi government policy told AFP on Friday.
Saudi Arabia will also not bow to the Houthis’ “military blackmail,” the source added, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter.
Saudi Arabia is ruling out negotiations on “any truce or ceasefire before the Yemeni government regains the territory it lost last month,” the source said.
“Saudi Arabia will not bow to blackmail,” the source added.

item.title: Bangladesh snatch late winner to beat Uzbekistan in U17 qualifiers
item.description:
Bangladesh scored a last-gasp goal to secure a 2-1 win against Uzbekistan in their AFC U17 Women’s Asian Cup China 2027 Qualifiers Group H match on Thursday.
Bangladesh will face off against the Philippines on Sunday to decide who will advance to the finals with Uzbekistan eliminated.
Uzbekistan, who lost 4-0 to the Philippines on Monday, knew they had to get something from this match to stay in the hunt for a place in the Finals but it was Bangladesh who drew first blood.
In the fourth minute, Fatema Akter swung a diagonal cross halfway across the pitch to Purnima Marma on the right flank, who then drew Mariya Khalkulova out of her goal before chipping the ball past the advancing keeper for the opener.
Bangladesh, however, undid their good work in the 17th minute when Airin Khatun dallied on the edge of her box, allowing Larangiz Lakaeva to dispossess her before slotting past Meghla Rani Roy.
The second half was evenly matched with both teams working hard to carve out chances.
Alpi Akter went close for the Tigresses when she dribbled into the box from the right but saw her effort saved by Khalkulova while at the other end, Meghla did well to parry Mubina Bakhtiyorova’s attempt from close range.
As Uzbekistan pushed forward late on, Bangladesh exploited the gaps in defence in the third minute of added time when Sorovi Rani sent Runa Akter through on goal to power home the winning goal.

item.title: Trump rules out new Iran attack before US midterm elections
item.description:
President Donald Trump on Thursday ruled out attacking Iran before the US midterm elections on November 3, saying Washington was holding "productive discussions" with Tehran.
Trump's post on his Truth Social platform followed a surge in oil prices on Thursday driven by media reports suggesting potential new US strikes prior to those elections.
"I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect...we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections," he wrote.
"We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran," he added, without providing additional details.
The Atlantic magazine reported on Wednesday that the White House had asked the Pentagon to develop options to strike Iranian targets that could be used before the midterms. The New York Times published a similar report on Thursday, saying the plans were being developed despite Trump's "ambivalence."
The rise in crude oil prices has also been fueled by persistent tensions in the Strait of Hormuz -- a strategic chokepoint for the global oil trade -- as well as hostilities between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
Polls suggest that US voters are strongly dissatisfied over rising fuel prices, linked to the conflict launched by the United States and Israel against Iran on February 28.
Brent North Sea crude, the international benchmark, rallied to as high as $105.88 a barrel before retreating to $104.28.
Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin promised Thursday to "do everything" to help end the Middle East war when he met Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian for talks ahead of a regional summit, Russian media reported.
"We are ready to do everything that is in our power to contribute to the settlement of this situation," Putin said after arriving in Turkmenistan for a summit of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) that starts Friday in the Caspian Sea resort of Avaza.
He added that Iran had made "real efforts to end the war," according to Russian news agencies.
Russia and Iran have reinforced diplomatic and military links since Russia launched its offensive in Ukraine in February 2022, becoming increasingly reliant on each other.
Trump has repeatedly insisted in recent weeks that the United States has effectively won the Iran war, despite ongoing unrest and a recent security threat that forced the withdrawal of American bombers from a base in England.
But Trump's claims that prices will fall as soon as the Iran war is over have so far fallen on deaf ears with voters.
The midterm elections will shape the final two years of Trump's presidential term as his Republican Party risks losing its current grip on Congress.
Although Trump is not on the ballot, he is holding numerous rallies in an attempt to limit the damage or even turn the political tide.
Trump has warned he faces a possible third impeachment if Democrats retake the House of Representatives, and the White House is preparing for a slew of investigations into corruption and abuse of power.
The US president also on Thursday sought to calm a furor over his comments at a rally earlier this week that Iran could "take out" the cities of Los Angeles and San Diego.
Trump, 80, blamed the "fake and artificial news" for misinterpreting the remarks, which Democrats pounced on.
"In actuality, what I was talking about was that a temporary increase in the price of Gasoline is a small price to pay for Iran not having a Nuclear Weapon and, if you want to see a big price, can you imagine what it would be like if they bombed San Diego and/or Los Angeles?" Trump said on Truth Social.

item.title: From Aibak’s horse messengers to the digital age: Rebirthing the post
item.description:
As the world celebrates World Post Day on October 9, many might assume that the relevance of postal services has faded in an era of instantaneous digital messages that travel thousands of miles at the touch of a fingertip.
Thanks to technology-induced transformations and value-added services, today we celebrate a global system that does far more than just deliver mail.
With over 660,000 post offices and 4.6 million staff across the globe, the postal network connects communities and provides essential services designed to leave no one behind.
This year’s theme, “One postal network, infinite possibilities,” reflects the role of the postal system as a trusted facilitator and a one-stop shop enabling people to participate in the economy and society—whether it is a young person opening a digital bank account, a family accessing virtual healthcare, a small business reaching global markets, or an elderly neighbor receiving a welfare check.
Crucially, these services are delivered in person, providing a real, human touchpoint in an increasingly digital world. As one of the oldest examples of multilateralism, global cooperation ensures messages and goods arrive even amid disasters, prompting United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres to invite the world to honor postal workers and the Universal Postal Union for all they do to connect our world.
“The postal system is one of the oldest examples of multilateralism in action, with global cooperation ensuring messages, goods and services arrive even amid disasters and emergencies. Today, let’s honour postal workers and the Universal Postal Union – and all they do to connect our world,” the UN Secretary-General says in message marking the day.
In Bangladesh, the Directorate of Posts is observing a nationwide Postal Service Week from today, featuring letter festivals, philatelic exhibitions, and postal fairs at educational institutions to engage the younger generation. As the nation joins the global observance of World Post Day 2026, the department is actively transforming its traditional operations into a modern, technology-driven logistics network.
The roots of this system trace back to the 13th century, when Qutb ud-Din Aibak, the Turkic general who founded the Delhi Sultanate, established the first recorded postal network in Bengal using horse messengers from Delhi. The system was further developed by Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq, as noted by Arabian travel writer Ibn Battuta, when postal officers also engaged in law enforcement. Further improvements were made under Sher Shah Suri, founder of the Suri Empire, who developed the Grand Trunk Road and established 1,700 postal houses with 3,400 runners, while Mughal Emperor Jahangir later introduced carrier pigeons to transport messages.
Following the East India Company’s takeover of Bengal, Robert Clive established a General Post Office in Kolkata on March 17, 1774, creating a network known as Clive’s Post that connected commercial hubs like Calcutta, Chittagong, Dhaka, Dinajpur, Murshidabad, Rajshahi, Rangpur, and Rajmahal. On October 1, 1854, the first postage stamps worth one anna and half anna were introduced, followed by the adoption of rail transport that same year and the launch of the Railway Mail Service in 1864. Roadside letter boxes were introduced between 1856 and 1857.
During the 1971 Liberation War, the provisional government established a postal service with 50 field offices near the Indian border in Mukti Bahini-controlled areas. Barrister Moudud Ahmed served as the first Postmaster General, and artist Biman Mullick designed the nation’s first eight stamps—including one featuring Sheikh Mujibur Rahman—which were subsequently outlawed by the Pakistani government.
Today, that historic framework has expanded into a vast network of over 8,000 post offices employing roughly 40,000 staff across Bangladesh. Faced with a sharp decline in personal correspondence—with annual mail volumes plummeting from over 400 million letters in the 1980s and 1990s to less than 50 million today—the department must realign its deliverables with tech-driven platforms to utilize its full potential.
According to its official site, the Bangladesh Post Office currently caters to 16 types of services, including ordinary and registered mail, Guaranteed Express Post, Express Mail Service, ordinary money orders, Electronic Money Transfer Service, postal cash cards, parcel services, Value Payable Post, Value Payable Letters, postage stamp sales, postal life insurance, savings banks, savings certificate operations, prize bond management, biri banderol printing, and the distribution of non-postal government stamps.
According to a recent ministry press release, the scope of these services is expanding through enhanced e-commerce capabilities, digital tracking, post pickup services, fulfillment centers, specialized transport for agricultural products, and entrepreneur-based franchise post offices.
Recent data shows that around 811 tonnes of goods have been transported via Speed Post since March 2026, making it an affordable lifeline for online businesses, farmers, and small enterprises. International parcel transportation is also growing; outbound volumes rose from 243 tonnes in the first three months of the 2025–26 fiscal year to 316 tonnes during the same period in the 2026–27 fiscal year, marking a 29.84 percent increase.
Furthermore, the postal service recently played a vital civic role by ensuring the exercise of voting rights through postal ballots for 1,533,683 expatriate and domestic voters during the 13th parliamentary election in February 2026, proving that this centuries-old institution remains deeply relevant to modern society.

item.title: DNCC launches campaign to repaint July graffiti on metro rail pillars
item.description:
Dhaka North City Corporation (DNCC) has launched a campaign to repaint graffiti commemorating the July uprising on metro rail pillars in Mirpur, inviting residents to take part in the initiative.
DNCC Administrator Md Shafiqul Islam inaugurated the “Let’s Remake July Graffiti” campaign on Friday.
The city corporation will provide paint, brushes and other necessary materials to participants, according to a DNCC statement.
Speaking at the inauguration, Shafiqul said the corporation had earlier announced a 72-hour deadline to remove posters from the metro rail pillars. The posters were removed ahead of the deadline with the help of local leaders, particularly those from Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal, Jatiyatabadi Swechchhasebak Dal and Jatiyatabadi Jubo Dal, he said.
He said the next step was to replace the posters with July graffiti to honour those who sacrificed their lives and contributed to the country’s history.
Shafiqul also announced plans to include an image of former prime minister Khaleda Zia on the pillars, citing her contribution to the July uprising.
Graffiti will also feature leaders of the July movement, including Chhatra Dal leaders and representatives of other political parties, he said.
“We will not politicize this initiative. We will paint graffiti to record each person’s contribution in the pages of history,” he added.

item.title: Police: DNA from crime-scene matches two accused in Rangpur family murder
item.description:
The DNA of the two suspects arrested in connection with the murders of former schoolteacher Ganapati Chakraborty and his family members in Rangpur has shown a “statistical match” to DNA collected from different pieces of evidence found at the scene, police have said.
Samples collected from date seeds, bitten cucumber pieces and cigarette filters found at the spot showed a match in laboratory tests, Rangpur Metropolitan Police Deputy Commissioner (Detective Branch) Sonaton Chakroborty said on Thursday night.
“Tests on the DNA samples collected from Siddhartha Das and Mugdha Das at the CID Forensic Lab in Dhaka matched the DNA found in the evidence,” he said.
According to sources, forensic tests had earlier detected male DNA in the date seeds, cucumber pieces and cigarette filters, but investigators had yet to identify whose DNA it was. The samples were subsequently compared with those collected from the two suspects.
On August 22, the bodies of Ganapati, 65, a former teacher of Rangpur Zilla School, his wife Pritilata Chakraborty Bala, 50, daughter Agami Chakraborty Prarthi, 25, and son Ayush Chakraborty Priyam, 12, were recovered from their locked home in Machhuapara of Rangpur city.
Within six hours of the murders, police arrested two suspects, Mugdha and Siddharth.
The two suspects were taken from Rangpur Central Jail to Dhaka on the night of September 20, and their DNA samples were collected at the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) office the following day.
Investigators collected more than 35 pieces of evidence from the scene, including a fruit knife, foil used for Yaba consumption, cigarette ends, cucumbers, dates, marks on a washbasin and writing found in a notebook belonging to one of the deceased children.
The items were sent for forensic examination in several phases.
Police had earlier said the suspects stayed inside the house after the killings and ate dates and cucumbers.
The DB is investigating the incident.

item.title: Attack on journos at RU: Probe panel recommends suspension of 4 students
item.description:
A probe committee at Rajshahi University (RU) has recommended suspending four students over an attack on journalists at Shaheed Ziaur Rahman Hall.
The committee has also recommended further investigation into allegations against four other students before taking action and issuing warnings to three others.
A five-member probe committee was formed to identify those involved in the incident at Shaheed Ziaur Rahman Hall on October 4, said Vice-Chancellor Prof Dr Md Faridul Islam while reading out the investigation report to journalists at the VC's conference room on Friday.
The university administration received the probe report around midnight on Thursday, he added.
The probe panel recommended suspending Vice President of RU unit of Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal (JCD) Ahsan Habib, Joint General Secretary Hasibul Hasan, General Secretary of Ziaur Rahman Hall Students' Union Ariful Islam and JCD activist Bishal Chakraborty, the VC said.
He said the committee recommended further investigation into the allegations against Rakibul Islam, assistant cultural affairs secretary of the RU Central Students' Union (Rucsu); Takbir Ahmed Emon, vice president of RU unit JCD; Syed Sajharul Islam, joint general secretary; and JCD activist Tanim Rahman before taking action.
The committee also recommended issuing warnings to Bulbul Rahman and Shariful Islam, vice-presidents of the university unit of JCD, and Shahriar Alam, assistant office secretary.
On October 4, journalists came under attack while performing their professional duties in front of Shaheed Ziaur Rahman Hall on the campus.
At least 10 people, including four journalists, were injured in the incident.
Following the attack, the university administration formed a five-member probe committee.
After a meeting with journalists, the VC directed the committee to submit its report within 72 hours.

item.title: Argentina friendlies no fairy tale for African footballers
item.description:
When Benin and Burkina Faso flew to Buenos Aires for friendlies against Argentina -- including superstar Lionel Messi's swansong-- it would have seemed like dreamland for players who rarely if ever rub shoulders with the aristocrats of the 'Beautiful Game'.
In reality, the organisation was a shambles, a member of the Benin delegation told AFP.
The flight to Buenos Aires took not hours but days. There was no hot water in the hotel. Training facilities were "not up to scratch".
And the African football associations invited didn't receive any of the profits from the match, which potentially generated millions of dollars in revenue and TV rights, he said.
Before the match, the state-owned daily La Nation in Cotonou looked forward breathlessly to the team "showcasing Benin to the whole world" and the national football association revelled in the "privilege" of being selected to play.
"I'm going to tell Messi, 'You are a god'," Benin defender Mohamed Tijani informed the Argentine press of the country's legendary No 10. "He's the best player in the world."
The Cheetahs lost 3-0.
Whilst there is no standard practice for organising international professional friendlies, smaller African teams generally rely on agencies to manage their away fixtures and don't necessarily make any profit from the games.
"African football associations accept these deals because everything is taken care of. It saves them having to find opponents and organise friendlies," explained an expert on African football who asked not to be named.
"But it's true the travel and accommodation arrangements are substandard."
The Burkina friendly turned into a farce.
On the eve of kick-off, the Stallions were still stranded in Morocco after their connecting flight to Buenos Aires was cancelled.
When organisers eventually found them a plane at the last minute, the senior squad was so annoyed it refused to board and Burkina ended up hastily despatching an under-23 team.
The young players arrived jet-lagged just a few hours before the match and were predictably thrashed 7-0 by this year’s World Cup finalists.
Piqued, Burkina's military ruler Ibrahim Traore complained the country's football was "in a sorry state" and threatened "significant decisions" to "remedy it".
"The next international window in November is fast approaching," Burkinabe Football Federation official Ibrahim Dianda warned on Facebook.
"If the relationship between the stakeholders doesn't change, we risk a repeat of these difficulties and the consequences could be even more regrettable," he wrote.
Fans want to know who is to blame for the humiliation.
Could it be the African federations that accept these one-sided deals?
Or the Argentine Football Association (AFA), which is accused by some of capitalising on its high profile and on appearances by Messi -- the country's most famous living export -- to maximise revenue?
Whatever the underlying motives, the AFA is in financial difficulty, faces a money laundering probe and has a president, Claudio Tapia, suspected of tax evasion.
In Argentina, some newspapers and social media channels pour scorn on what they sniffily refer to as "chatarra" (cheap, low-quality) fixtures.
Messi's side also played Mauritania (110th in the FIFA rankings) and Zambia (91st) in World Cup warm-ups this year, beating them 2-1 and 5-0 respectively.
His team also pocketed a hefty sum -- several million dollars -- for travelling to Luanda in November 2025 for a friendly marking Angola's 50th Independence Day celebrations.
An assist and a goal by the eight-time Ballon d'Or winner ensured a 2-0 victory over the African side.
In reaction to the uproar in Burkina over the national team's treatment, match organiser Eurodata Sport issued a terse statement shared online by the AFA that it had "honoured its contractual commitments".
They declined to respond to AFP's request for comment.

item.title: More than just football: How scandal-tainted City led Manchester's rebirth
item.description:
Standing behind the counter of his fish-and-chip shop near the Etihad Stadium, Sailish Parekh says the transformation of east Manchester over the past two decades has been remarkable.
Manchester City "has not only just been a football club for the area. It's a bit of a saviour, to be honest," he told AFP.
Before City -- now embroiled in the biggest financial scandal to hit football's cash-rich Premier League -- moved to the area it was "very deprived" with high rates of unemployment, he said.
Since the club's takeover by deep-pocketed Abu Dhabi investors in 2008, long-neglected districts between the stadium and the city centre have become symbols of the northern city's rebirth.
Decades of decline linked to deindustrialisation have been reversed.
In neighbourhoods such as Ancoats and New Islington, red-brick warehouses still stand as reminders of Manchester's industrial past.
But many disused mills and factories have given way to apartment blocks, trendy cafes and co-working spaces.
Software engineer Simon Martin, 44, who lives in Ancoats, recounted how a cab driver told him he would have hesitated once to pick him up, when the area was riddled with crime.
Today, Martin praises the "really nice community" with "more young families moving in", although soaring rents have pushed out some lower-income residents.
The transformation reflects the influence of Manchester City and its owner, Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG), controlled by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, a member of the United Arab Emirates royal family.
The Emirati investors have not just turned City into one of Europe's dominant football clubs.
They have also poured money into property development, building homes and commercial spaces on council-owned land leased under favourable terms.
The partnership is centred on Manchester Life, a property company created jointly between ADUG and the council in 2014, but it has drawn criticism over transparency and profit distribution.
In a 2024 study, University of Sheffield researchers argued the arrangement primarily enabled the ADUG group to lock in rising land values.
- 'Our Eiffel Tower' -
The city council rejects the criticism, saying it secured "the best overall deal" at a time when investors were scarce after the 2007-2008 global financial crisis.
According to the council, the partnership delivered around 1,500 homes and nearly 2,800 square metres (30,100 square feet) of commercial space.
The debate has resurfaced after the Premier League announced last week that an independent commission had found the club guilty on more than 100 charges of breaking financial rules.
It has been accused of artificially inflating revenues and reduced reported costs by more than £900 million ($1.2 billion) between 2009 and 2018.
No sanction has yet been announced but City could face substantial points deductions, a fine or even expulsion from the Premier League. It could also face compensation claims from other clubs.
City insists it has done nothing wrong.
With both Manchester City and rivals Manchester United having huge international draw, football is one of the city's defining assets, said Subrahmaniam Krishnan-Harihara, head of research at the Greater Manchester Chamber of Commerce.
"This is our Eiffel Tower. I think without football, the brand value would not be this big," he told AFP.
According to consultants EY, Premier League-related activity generates around £1.6 billion ($2.1 billion) in annual revenues across Greater Manchester.
The city also attracts about 1.7 million overseas visitors each year.
Manchester City was a "catalyst" for infrastructure projects, including the expansion of the tram network, said Krishnan-Harihara.
- Overcoming austerity -
Club officials say more than £700 million has been invested since 2008 in the Etihad Campus and surrounding districts, where sports facilities, a sixth-form college, a velodrome, retail developments and the Co-op Arena concert venue have emerged.
The Abu Dhabi investors were "key", said Georgina Blakeley, a professor at the University of Huddersfield who highlighted the impact of the 2007-2008 crash.
"You really get that turning off of the tap of regeneration activity ... and austerity hit cities like Manchester particularly hard," she said.
The Manchester Life project became part of the so-called "Manchester model", an urban development strategy championed by the council in the early 2000s and backed by Andy Burnham, the Greater Manchester mayor from 2017 to 2026 who is now UK prime minister.
Burnham sparked controversy recently when he said he would be "really concerned" should the Emirati owners walk away over the finance charges.
His office later sought to clarify the remarks, insisting "there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules".
But Krishnan-Harihara believes any sanctions imposed on the club are unlikely to inflict lasting damage on Manchester's economic prospects.
"The foreign direct investment pool is actually widespread because there are other countries, other sectors which are also attracting investment," he said.
Fish-and-chip shop owner Parekh agreed. Manchester is now "quite a lot" more than "the two football clubs," he argued.

item.title: Iran president says peace talks will only succeed without ‘pressure, threats’
item.description:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Friday at a regional summit in Turkmenistan that peace negotiations will only succeed without “pressure and threats,” with the months-long Middle East war locked in a stalemate.
“Dialogue holds meaning and a chance of success only when based on mutual respect and mutual commitments, and when devoid of pressure and threat,” he said during his speech at the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) summit.
“Negotiation conducted in the shadow of force is not negotiation, it is imposition and coercion,” he said, warning that sanctions on Iran would affect “regional trade, connectivity, energy, and order.”
The comments came as Pezeshkian on Monday said talks with the United States to end the war that began in late February were worthless and only resulted in renewed attacks.
“With an enemy that everyday resorts to assassination, sanctions, pressure and threats, and that breaks its commitments, negotiations are meaningless,” he noted.
The war started with US and Israeli attacks on Iran, while Washington and Tehran were locked in negotiations on Iran’s nuclear program.
The warring parties agreed a memorandum of understanding in June that spelled out a framework for a permanent resolution to the conflict, but Iranian attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz prompted a resumption of US military operations.
Negotiations have effectively been at an impasse since then, and recent indirect talks between the US and Iran on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly failed to produce a breakthrough.
Washington in recent weeks has dialed back military operations in favor of economic pressure and has not struck Iran since September 1.
The United States and Israel have said the war is necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons -- a goal Tehran has long denied pursuing.
The focus shifted to reopening the Strait of Hormuz after its closure sent shockwaves through global energy markets.
Iran has sought to impose its control over the vital shipping lane since the start of the war, striking vessels that attempt to transit without its authorization.
The US has imposed its own counterblockade of Iranian ports and has also struck vessels it accuses of violating it.

item.title: Pentagon: US to livestream Fort Hood shooter’s execution
item.description:
The execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, who shot and killed 13 people at Ford Hood in 2009, will be livestreamed, the US military said Thursday.
The confirmation came a day after US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had said Hasan’s execution, which is slated for December 3, would be done in “public.”
Pentagon officials added that more details on the execution would follow.
In a video posted on X by official Pentagon accounts, Hegseth had said Wednesday that Hasan would get “a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public.”
Hegseth was speaking to right-wing influencer Jack Posobiec on board the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, which ended a nearly 10-month deployment on Thursday.
“People need to understand that there’s serious consequence for these types of things,” Hegseth said.
Hasan’s execution will be the first by the US military since 1961, and will be the first to be done by firing squad since World War II.
Hegseth added: “I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II, which was win.”
US Army psychiatrist Hasan killed 13 people and wounded 32 others at Fort Hood, Texas.
A military court sentenced him to death in 2013.
During his trial, Hasan said he had perpetrated the shooting to protect Taliban members in Afghanistan from US troops.
The announcement that Hasan will be executed by firing squad comes amid the fallout of the botched execution of Christa Pike.

item.title: Malaysia closes schools in capital, parts of country due to haze
item.description:
Malaysia closed schools in Kuala Lumpur and other parts of the country on Friday, as haze from fires in neighboring Indonesia again plunged local air quality to among the world’s worst.
Toxic smoke from peatland as well as forest fires has shrouded towns and cities in the region for more than a month, sending respiratory complaints skyrocketing.
The school closures came as Malaysia’s leader discussed the choking smoke with his Indonesian counterpart and called for an urgent regional meeting.
Kuala Lumpur’s air quality worsened on Friday to hit a reading of around 224 on the index of Swiss-based monitor IQAir, which said that change pushed Malaysia’s capital past Singapore to be the “most polluted global major city.”
Malaysia’s Education Minister Fadhlina Sidek said she has instructed full school closures in four states and two federal territories as well as one partial closure in the central Pahang State.
Schools were also closed on Friday in three districts in western Perak State.
Malaysia’s education ministry could not immediately be reached for comment on whether schools will reopen on Monday.
“In the future, we will ensure that any decision to close schools is notified in advance so that parents have sufficient time to prepare,” Fadhlina said late on Thursday.
Malaysia’s King Sultan Ibrahim weighed in on the matter on Thursday, saying schools should be closed as air quality readings reached 150 or higher on the Air Pollutant Index (API).
“Appropriate measures must be taken by the relevant ministries and agencies to protect schoolchildren and students, including senior citizens and patients with respiratory illnesses,” King Sultan Ibrahim said.
Under Malaysian guidelines, API readings above 100 are classified as unhealthy, above 200 as very unhealthy, above 300 as hazardous, while readings beyond 500 constitute the threshold for declaring a local emergency.
Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Thursday he discussed the fire situation with the Indonesian leader Prabowo Subianto.
“The haze issue is indeed at a worrying level. And I have personally contacted President Prabowo,” Anwar said.
“And he also agreed to take the necessary steps,” Anwar said, without going into specific details.
He said Malaysia has been taking measures to combat the haze, including increasing attempts to trigger rain via cloud seeding.
Indonesia’s government said “regular dialogue between the leaders is a natural part of the close relations” of the two nations.
Experts said the flames are being fanned by a turbo-charged El Nino weather phenomenon, causing the worst pollution conditions in years.
Anwar said he asked Malaysia’s Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan to contact the 11-nation Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ secretariat for an urgent meeting between environmental ministers to discuss the matter.
“So these are all the steps we are taking, but we are monitoring and will try the measures that we ought to take next,” Anwar said.
Singapore’s air quality levels too dipped into the “very unhealthy” range with a reading of 209 on the Air Quality Index in Friday afternoon, according to the IQAir website.
The AQI converts measurements of pollutants into a single figure indicating air quality and potential health risks.
Readings above 150 are classified as unhealthy, while levels above 300 are considered hazardous.

item.title: UN calls for inclusive mental health care on World Mental Health Day
item.description:
The United Nations has reaffirmed the expertise and leadership of people with lived experience of mental health challenges on World Mental Health Day.
This year’s theme, “Lived Experiences Heard: Real Voices, Real Change,” highlights how people are often excluded from decisions affecting their lives, despite their insights being essential to developing effective services and policies.
The UN said it is particularly important for young people facing economic uncertainty, climate anxiety and online harms, as well as people affected by conflicts and humanitarian crises, where disrupted services can worsen psychological distress.
More than 80% of countries currently provide mental health services in psychiatric hospitals, while many people with lived experience prefer to recover at home and in their communities, it said.
The UN has further called on governments to replace exclusion with partnership and invest in community-centred mental health care.
It has also urged renewed efforts to address stigma and build mental health systems grounded in dignity and human rights for all.

item.title: Tanzil Misbah Doulat on power of listeners ‘Love and Prayer’
item.description:
“I am sincerely grateful to everyone who has been listening to my songs, loving my work and supporting me from the very beginning. I want to promise that as long as I continue making music, I will always try to win a place in listeners’ hearts with every song I release. Their love and prayers are the greatest strength behind my journey.”
These are the words of popular singer Tanzil Misbah Doulat, who has already made a strong impression on listeners with his melodious voice.
Tanzil Misbah Doulat’s full name is Tanzil Misbah Doulat Khan. He was born and raised in Danga Union of Palash upazila in Narsingdi. He spent most of his childhood there. From an early age, Misbah developed a special passion for music and singing.
The singer began his musical journey with the song Emon Ekta Manush, which received a warm response from listeners following its release. Encouraged by the response, he went on to release several more original songs.
Among his popular tracks are Emon Ekta Manush, Lal Shari, Maya Kore Bole, Mayar Duniya, Chand Bodone, Tota Pakhi, Jan Re, Ayre Moyna and Firbo Na Tomar Shohore, among others.
At present, he is working on an album as well as several original songs. Around 10 new projects are currently in the works, all of which will be released for listeners at the appropriate time, the singer said.
Misbah has also had the opportunity to collaborate with several established artists. He has recorded a duet with Avanti Sithi and has also worked on duet songs with Kazi Shuvo, Lutfor Hasan, Mohammad Milon and Jisan Khan Shuvo. So far, the singer has released more than 15 original songs.
Asked about his passion for music, he said, “Music is not just a profession for me; it is my love, my emotion and the greatest medium through which I express myself. I always want to make songs that are not only relevant today but continue to live in people’s hearts for years to come.”
He added, “My biggest dream is to present Bangla music to the world on a larger scale. One of my main goals is for my songs to reach Bangla-speaking people in different parts of the world, beyond the borders of Bangladesh. I believe good music and genuine emotions have no boundaries.”
“I want every one of my songs to become connected with some emotion in the listeners’ lives. I hope there comes a time when, even many years later, someone listens to one of my songs and is reminded of a particular memory from their life. I want my songs to be more than just songs to my listeners—to become a part of their lives. That would be my greatest achievement.”
Looking ahead, Misbah wants to work on better songs, explore new forms of music and take on diverse musical projects. He also hopes to continually reinvent himself and contribute to the enrichment of Bangla music in his own way.

item.title: Rakibul Hasan builds career across music, digital distribution and Islamic content
item.description:
From Sandwip in Chittagong to the evolving world of digital music, Rakibul Hasan has developed a career that brings together music creation, digital distribution, artist rights, copyright protection and a growing focus on Islamic nasheeds and Quran recitations.
Rakibul Hasan was born on 12 April 2000 in Sandwip, Chittagong, Bangladesh.
His journey into music and digital media began at around the age of 18, when he first became interested in music beat production, digital content and the process of distributing music through online platforms.
What began as a creative interest gradually developed into a broader professional direction.
During the early stages of his career, Hasan spent time exploring how music was created, presented and released. Alongside making music beats, he occasionally worked with digital content and began learning about the infrastructure behind independent music distribution.
As his experience increased, he became increasingly interested in what happens after a song is completed.
For an independent artist, finishing a recording is only one stage of a much larger process. The music still needs to be distributed, accurately identified, connected to the correct artist profile and presented with consistent metadata across multiple digital services. Questions involving copyright, master ownership, licensing, royalties and distribution permissions can also determine what happens to a recording in the long term.
Hasan’s interest in these areas eventually became just as important as his interest in creating music.
Rather than limiting himself to a single role within the industry, he began building experience on both sides of music: as a creator and as someone working with the systems that support artists after the creative process is complete.
One of his earlier notable personal projects is “Prem Amar,” released through his own channel. Hasan also appeared as a model in the project, giving him experience in the visual and creative side of music production.
Over the years, he has been involved in more than 30 music projects.
His recent releases include Teri Ada Ka Nasha, Tu Aaya Na, Teri Kami Reh Gayi, Kuch Der Ka Saath, Teri Aankhon Ka Zehar, Tere Ishq Mein Gehra, Tere Naam Se, Aadhi Raat Ka Nasha, Bheegi Raat Mein Tu, Raat Bhar Tera Nasha, Teri Raaton Ka Nasha, Raat Bhar Tera Naam, Chhod Aaya Main, Tere Baad Bhi, Main Khud Se Haar Gaya, Bas Tum Mere Paas Raho, Tu Meri Rooh Ka Raaz and Rangrez Tera Pyaar.
His work also includes Bengali-language releases such as Rokte Lekha Joy Bangla, Sandwiper Kanna and Joy Bangla.
Hasan is continuing to develop his personal catalog while also exploring collaborations beyond Bangladesh. One of his upcoming projects is “Alone,” being prepared for his own channel with Indian artist Akash Sen involved in the project.
For Hasan, working with artists across borders reflects one of the most important changes in the modern music industry.
Digital platforms have made geography less restrictive for creators. An artist in Bangladesh can collaborate with someone in India, the Middle East, Europe or another market and make the resulting work available to listeners internationally.
However, Hasan believes global access brings new responsibilities as well.
As music becomes easier to distribute internationally, creators need to understand more about how their catalogs are managed, who controls their rights and how information connected to a release is maintained.
This growing interest in the business side of music became an important foundation for Rahat Music.
Rahat Music Distribution operates through Rahat Music Limited, a company registered in the United Kingdom under Company Number 17154141.
The company works in areas connected with digital music distribution, publishing administration, royalty management, copyright protection and anti-piracy support.
For Hasan, Rahat Music developed around a problem he had repeatedly seen while working in the industry: many talented independent artists understand the creative side of music but have limited knowledge of the business and technical processes that follow a recording.
A professional release involves much more than simply uploading an audio file.
Tracks need accurate metadata. Recordings may require ISRCs, while releases can require UPCs. Artist identities need to be mapped correctly. Ownership and licensing need to be documented. Distribution permissions should be clear, and agreements between artists, labels and rights holders should establish who is authorized to do what.
If these issues are ignored at the beginning, problems can appear much later.
A track may be delivered by more than one distributor. An artist profile may be mapped incorrectly. A third party may attempt to monetize a recording. Revenue can become disputed, or different parties may make conflicting claims over the same master.
Hasan believes greater awareness can help independent creators avoid many of these problems.
“Creating the music is only one part of the journey,” Hasan says. “An artist should also understand where the recording is being distributed, who has permission to distribute it, who controls the master and how the rights are being managed.”
That philosophy has become an important part of Rahat Music’s direction.
Hasan does not see digital distribution simply as the process of delivering a track to streaming platforms. He sees it as part of a larger relationship between artists, rights holders, distributors and the digital services where audiences ultimately hear the music.
This perspective has also made copyright protection an increasingly important part of his work.
The growth of streaming, social media and short-form video platforms has given musicians unprecedented opportunities to reach audiences. At the same time, digital technology has made recordings easier to copy, redistribute and monetize without proper authorization.
Independent rights holders can be particularly vulnerable.
A recording may appear under an unauthorized artist name, be distributed through another company or be uploaded to social platforms without the knowledge of the original rights holder.
Once such content spreads across multiple services, resolving the issue can become complicated.
For Hasan, clear documentation is one of the most important forms of protection.
Agreements should establish who owns a recording. Distribution rights should be clearly authorized. Revenue splits should be documented. Artists should know whether an agreement is exclusive or non-exclusive and understand how long any permission remains valid.
“Artists should understand their rights before there is a dispute,” Hasan says. “Clear ownership and clear agreements can prevent many problems later.”
Alongside its wider distribution activities, Rahat Music has developed a particularly strong interest in Islamic audio content.
The company works with Islamic nasheeds, Quran recitations and other faith-based audio releases, while continuing to work with music from broader categories.
For Hasan, Islamic content is not simply another section of a digital catalog.
He believes it requires a more specialized approach because of the nature of the material and the expectations of both creators and listeners.
Quran recitation is one example.
A Quran recitation needs to be presented with care. Surah titles, Arabic text, reciter information and other metadata should be accurate and consistent across platforms.
Incorrect information may create confusion and can be particularly sensitive when religious content is involved.
Nasheed releases can also require a different understanding from conventional mainstream music.
Some nasheed artists choose to work entirely without musical instruments. Others may use vocal layering, humming or acapella-style arrangements depending on their artistic and religious approach.
Hasan believes distributors working with this category should understand and respect those choices.
“Islamic content should be handled professionally, but it should also be handled respectfully,” Hasan says. “Correct attribution, accurate titles and proper information are important.”
The potential audience for Islamic audio is international.
Quran recitations and nasheeds are heard across South Asia, the Middle East, Southeast Asia, Africa, Europe, North America and other parts of the world.
Digital platforms have made it possible for an independent Quran reciter or nasheed artist to reach listeners far beyond the community in which the content was originally created.
Hasan sees significant potential in this area.
Many Islamic creators operate independently and may not have access to the same level of digital infrastructure, rights-management support or industry knowledge available to artists working with larger labels.
Rahat Music’s focus on Islamic content is intended to help address that gap.
The goal is to create a professional route through which nasheed artists and Quran reciters can distribute their recordings internationally while maintaining a clearer understanding of ownership, metadata and rights.
At the same time, Hasan does not want Rahat Music to be viewed solely as an Islamic-content company.
Its wider activities include working with independent artists and rights holders across different forms of music.
The Islamic focus represents an area of specialization rather than a limitation on the company’s wider ambitions.
That balance also reflects Hasan’s own career.
His personal music includes releases in different languages and styles, while his work through Rahat Music has given him a particular interest in nasheeds, Quran recitation and religious audio.
For him, the modern digital music industry has room for both.
Another important part of Hasan’s vision is helping independent artists reach international audiences.
Traditionally, access to major music markets often depended on established labels, physical distribution networks and local industry relationships.
Streaming has changed that structure.
An independent artist can now release a track from Bangladesh and potentially reach listeners in numerous countries through the same global digital ecosystem.
However, Hasan believes simply making a song available internationally does not automatically mean that the artist’s career is being managed professionally.
As a catalog grows, accurate metadata becomes more important.
Correct artist mapping becomes more important.
Ownership records become more important.
Royalty tracking and licensing become more important.
For this reason, Hasan wants Rahat Music to develop beyond basic delivery and become a broader music-services operation.
The company’s United Kingdom registration is part of the formal structure behind that ambition.
Through Rahat Music Limited, registered under Company Number 17154141, Hasan is working toward building an internationally oriented business connected to independent creators, music rights and digital distribution.
He believes the company’s future should include relationships with artists and rights holders in Bangladesh, the Middle East, South Asia and other international markets.
But for Hasan, international growth is not only about adding more countries.
It is also about building professional standards that can function across borders.
When recordings involve multiple artists, producers, labels and territories, clear rights become increasingly important.
Hasan believes younger musicians should learn about these areas early in their careers.
Many people enter music because they know how to sing, compose, perform or produce. They may not initially understand concepts such as master rights, publishing, distribution licenses or royalty splits.
Hasan does not believe every artist needs to become a lawyer or music-business specialist. But he believes creators should know enough to understand the agreements connected to their own work.
They should know whether they own their masters.
They should know what rights they are giving to a distributor.
They should know whether a deal is exclusive.
And they should maintain records connected to their catalogs.
Hasan also encourages new artists to think beyond short-term popularity.
The modern music industry often places heavy attention on views, streams, trends and social-media numbers.
A song can attract attention quickly and disappear just as quickly.
Hasan believes a sustainable career requires something more durable.
Skills, knowledge, ownership, consistency and a recognizable creative identity are more important over time.
“Popularity can change very quickly,” Hasan says. “But your skills, your catalog and your understanding of the industry remain with you.”
His own professional journey reflects that gradual approach.
He began with music beats and digital content.
That interest expanded into distribution.
Distribution led him to learn more about copyright, rights management and catalog administration.
Those experiences eventually became part of the development of Rahat Music.
Today, at 26, Hasan continues to work across both the creative and business sides of the industry.
As a creator, he intends to continue releasing his own music and developing collaborations with artists from different markets.
As an entrepreneur, he wants to expand Rahat Music’s work with independent musicians, nasheed performers, Quran reciters and rights holders.
He also wants copyright protection and anti-piracy support to remain an important part of the company’s long-term development.
For Hasan, the ambition is not simply to build a large catalog or increase the number of releases connected with the company.
The larger goal is to create an environment in which artists have a clearer understanding of what happens to their work.
That means international distribution, but also ownership.
It means streaming, but also royalties.
It means expanding a catalog, but also maintaining accurate metadata.
And it means helping artists reach audiences while protecting the rights connected to what they create.
For Islamic content creators, Hasan believes the same principle should apply.
Nasheed performers and Quran reciters should be able to access professional digital infrastructure without losing sight of the religious, cultural and creative nature of their recordings.
From his beginnings in Sandwip, Chattogram, to his growing involvement in international digital music, Rakibul Hasan has developed a career that extends well beyond the beat-making work that first brought him into the industry.
His own music keeps him connected to the creative process, while Rahat Music gives him an opportunity to work with the systems that exist behind every professional release.
His long-term ambition is to bring those two sides together.
Hasan wants to continue developing his career as a music creator while building Rahat Music into a platform through which independent artists, nasheed performers and Quran reciters can distribute their work internationally, understand their rights and maintain greater control over the content they create.
For him, the combination of creativity, technology, ownership and artist independence is not simply part of the music industry’s present. It is also where he believes its future is heading.

item.title: The unheard notes
item.description:
When Louis Armstrong landed in Léopoldville (now Kinshasa) in October 1960, his trumpet was meant to herald American benevolence. Instead, as Johan Grimonprez’s electrifying documentary Soundtrack to a Coup d ’É tat reveals.
It provided cover for a darker symphony: the plot against Patrice Lumumba, the democratically elected prime minister of the newly independent Congo, in which the CIA and Belgium played their parts.
This isn’t just a film about history; it is a 150-minute indictment of how art, politics, and empire colluded in what Grimonprez calls a “cool war,” where jazz legends became pawns in a geopolitical chess game.
Lumumba’s Congo was born in 1960 amid a wave of African liberation movements. Rich in uranium (the very ore that fuelled America’s atomic bombs), the nation represented both hope and a threat.
As Grimonprez’s collage of archival footage shows, Lumumba’s vision--a sovereign Congo aligned with the Non-Aligned Movement--challenged Western hegemony. His assassination in January 1961, orchestrated by Belgian and U S operatives with UN complicity, was not merely a political murder; it was the crushing of a decolonial dream.
The film’s genius lies in its dissonant counterpoint: the exuberance of jazz.
Armstrong’s “La Vie en Rose” underscores Belgian looting; Nina Simone’s “The Ballad of Hollis Brown” scores CIA cables about Lumumba’s elimination.
Jazz, born from Black resistance in America, was weaponized by the same empire that suppressed its creators. The State Department’s “Jazz Ambassadors” program—featuring Dizzy Gillespie, Armstrong, and Simone--sent musicians to Africa as cultural diplomats. Unbeknownst to them, their tours provided cover for intelligence operations. White agents moved freely in their entourage, surveilling leftist movements while crowds swayed to “Hello, Dolly!”.
Grimonprez, a Belgian director confronting his nation’s colonial sins, refuses simplistic binaries.
His film exposes jazz musicians’ complicity and their rebellion. Armstrong, initially a willing ambassador, later threatened to renounce his citizenship over U.S. racism.
Abbey Lincoln and Max Roach, whose “We Insist! Freedom Now Suite” became an anthem for liberation and stormed the UN Security Council in 1961, demanding justice for Lumumba. In one haunting sequence, their protest--met with security dragnets--intercuts with Khrushchev pounding his shoe at the UN, railing against imperial hypocrisy.
The juxtaposition is quintessential Grimonprez: history as a cacophonous jam session where power, not melody, dictates the rhythm.
The film’s structural audacity mirrors jazz improvisation. It leaps from 1950s Brussels to contemporary Tesla ads, linking Congo’s plundered minerals (then uranium, now cobalt for smartphones) to modern capitalism.
Animated octopuses--symbols of colonial entanglement--spread tentacles across maps; grainy footage of elephants dumped into cargo holds mirrors Lumumba’s body being dissolved in acid. This isn’t didactic history; it’s sensory overload, forcing viewers to feel colonialism’s violence.
Not every note resonates. At 150 minutes, the film occasionally buckles under its ambitions. A segment showing John Coltrane’s face without sound during Congo’s bloodshed feels exploitative, reducing the saxophonist to a political prop. The dense weave of timelines--Malcolm X at the OAU, Khrushchev at Disneyland--can disorient. Yet these flaws stem from Grimonprez’s refusal to simplify. As the Arts Fuse notes, this is “an enormous undertaking with no comparables”.
Soundtrack to a Coup d ’É tat transcends historical documentary. By juxtaposing Lumumba’s speeches with ads for iPhones (dependent on Congolese cobalt), Grimonprez screams a truth Western comfort relies on forgetting: colonialism never ended; it rebranded.
When Tesla touts its “ethical batteries” over footage of child miners, the hypocrisy lands like a gut punch.
The film’s power lies in reclaiming jazz not as a tool of empire, but as a language of resistance. Lincoln’s wail on “Triptych: Prayer/Protest/Peace” becomes a dirge for Lumumba; Gillespie’s sly grin as he corrects Khrushchev’s “We will bury you” mistranslation (“He said I love you!”) embodies art’s subversive wit. In these moments, Grimonprez argues that while jazz was co-opted, its essence--improvisation, freedom, collective voice--remains inherently revolutionary.
Five years in production, funded across four European nations, Soundtrack to a Coup d ’É tat is itself an act of atonement. Belgium, the film reminds us, privatized Congo’s mines three days before granting independence.
By embedding this confession within a sonic tapestry of joy and rage, Grimonprez does more than document--he orchestrates a reckoning.
As the credits roll over Coltrane’s “Alabama,” we’re left with Lumumba’s unheeded warning: “Dead, living, free, or in prison--it is not I who counts. It is the Congo.” In an age of forever wars and invisible exploitation, this film is a flare shot into our collective conscience. The soundtrack of empire still plays, but Grimonprez hands us the mute button--and the responsibility to press it.
Soundtrack to a Coup d ’É tat is now streaming and available on demand. Its dissonance is a necessary antidote to the lullabies of forgetting.
Zakir Kibria is a Bangladeshi writer, policy analyst and entrepreneur based in Kathmandu.

item.title: ‘Crazy Rich Asians’ to return as HBO series
item.description:
HBO is developing an 8-episode drama series based on “Crazy Rich Asians,” bringing back several cast members from the 2018 romantic comedy.
Constance Wu, Henry Golding and Ronny Chieng will return as series regulars, while Michelle Yeoh will reprise her role in a recurring capacity. The series will continue the story following the events of the original film.
Based on Kevin Kwan’s bestselling novels, the show will explore the lives and relationships of its central characters and expand on the world introduced in the film.
Adele Lim, who co-wrote the 2018 adaptation, will serve as showrunner and executive producer. Kwan, director Jon M Chu, and producers Nina Jacobson and Brad Simpson will also serve as executive producers.
The original film followed Rachel Chu, played by Wu, an American-born Chinese professor who discovers the wealth and complicated family background of her boyfriend, Nick Young, played by Golding. Yeoh portrayed Nick’s mother, Eleanor Young, while Chien played his cousin Eddie Cheng.
Released in 2018, “Crazy Rich Asians” grossed more than $239 million worldwide and featured a predominantly Asian cast.
The series follows years of uncertainty over a planned film sequel. Production is scheduled to begin in 2027, while HBO has yet to announce a release date.

item.title: Emmy Awards to leave broadcast TV after 79 years
item.description:
The Emmy Awards will stream exclusively on Prime Video from 2027 to 2032 under a new six-year agreement with the Television Academy.
The deal marks the first time in the awards’ 79-year history that the ceremony will not air on broadcast television. The event will be available globally and free to watch, including for viewers without a Prime subscription.
Prime Video may also stream other Television Academy programmes, including the Hall of Fame and Television Academy Honors ceremonies. The platform for the Creative Arts Emmys has not yet been announced.
Television Academy Chair Cris Abrego told The Hollywood Reporter that the agreement offered an opportunity to rethink the broadcast model rather than simply renew the previous deal.
Abrego said the annual rotation among the four major US broadcast networks often meant starting over with a new partner, affecting producers, creative decisions and brand partnerships.
The Emmy Awards have previously aired on ABC, CBS, Fox and NBC. The 2026 Primetime Emmy Awards aired on NBC on September 14, with Peacock serving as the streaming partner.

item.title: US: Bangladesh steps up anti-trafficking efforts but gaps persist
item.description:
The government of Bangladesh convicted fewer traffickers and did not take adequate steps to address internal trafficking crimes, which remained pervasive, said the United States in its latest report released on Thursday.
The government of Bangladesh does not fully meet the minimum standards for the elimination of trafficking but is making significant efforts to do so, said the report.
The government demonstrated overall increasing efforts compared with the previous reporting period; therefore, Bangladesh remained on Tier 2, the report said.
These efforts included passing the Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking and Smuggling of Migrants Ordinance 2026 to strengthen the legal framework to combat trafficking, increasing investigations and prosecutions, updating the human trafficking crime and victim identification guidelines, and piloting a digital NRM to increase timeliness and coordination of referrals to protection services.
The government also strengthened protections for migrant workers to reduce vulnerabilities to trafficking.
However, the government did not meet the minimum standards in several key areas.
The government identified fewer victims, and victim protection and reintegration efforts remained insufficient, particularly for Rohingya refugees and returning Bangladeshi migrant workers.
Additionally, the government continued to permit worker-paid recruitment fees that rendered many migrant workers indebted, increasing their vulnerability to trafficking.
Spokesman at the US Department of State Thomas Tommy Pigott said human trafficking is a direct assault on the values of freedom and dignity that define America.
The 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report reveals new ways criminal organizations and repressive regimes use this abhorrent practice for financial gain.
The report also called for accountability for governments that fail to punish traffickers and protect their citizens.
The Trump Administration will use all available tools to fight traffickers and their enablers and bring them to justice, said the spokesman.
